newsitem.title: GERMANY: American-style mall opens in Germany.
newsitem.headline: American-style mall opens in Germany.

text.p: A huge American-style shopping mall opening in Germany's industrial heartland on Thursday aims to alter habits in consumption, entertainment and service in a country where customers have never come first.

The Centro mall in Oberhausen, Europe's biggest shopping and leisure complex, will only succeed if shoppers find this cheery temple of consumption differs enough from grumpy service found in local shops to merit a long car journey, owners say.

"Customer service in Germany has never been optimal, to say the least," said managing director Hans Matthijsse as workers put finishing touches on the mammoth 2.2 billion German mark ($1.5 billion) project.

"We aim to change that here," he said, watching a helicopter lower a giant globe onto the roof of a Planet Hollywood restaurant at the complex, near the city of Essen and less than 62 miles (100 km) from the Dutch border.

"The sales staffs are taking special training courses to learn to love their jobs, to treat customers as guests and not a nuisance," he said. "It is more than service with a smile. It is newfound motivation."
In a nation infamous for rude clerks, a woefully under-developed service industry, and rigid shop-closing laws, the "Centro Neue Mitte Oberhausen" is promising a lot.

But even before local politicians officially open it on Thursday, the mall with its 220 shops, 50 restaurants, nine cinemas, two hotels and 11,500 parking spots has already fascinated Germans with its superlatives:

-- It is Europe's largest shopping centre and leisure park, with 84,000 square yards of floor space spread out over a campus-like park of 996,000 square yards of grassy greens, tree-lined playgrounds, rivers and lakes.
-- It is the size of 200 soccer fields and Germany's second largest construction project, employing 5,000 workers, trailing only the enormous Berlin Potsdamer Platz construction site.
-- It was erected in just two years in a country where it can take many years to design and build even a parking lot.

-- It was built on the site of a steel mill closed in 1987 and includes a sports arena and concert hall that seats 12,500, a glass and steel structure so impressive that singer Gloria Estefan switched an already scheduled concert to the new hall.

-- It will create 10,000 jobs in a region plagued by double-digit unemployment and, its proponents hope, spawn a new trend in retailing in Germany, where such developments have long been blocked by inner-city retailers.
"No one has ever built anything like this in Europe," said Petra Doden, spokeswoman for the mall that more resembles a small American city than a German shopping boulevard.
She expects 30 million people per year to descend upon the mall on the outskirts of Oberhausen, once a gray and decaying city in the heart of the densely populated Ruhr Valley.

Centro is a few notches below the huge palaces of consumerism found across the United States and Canada. The largest U.S. centre, the Mall of America in Bloomington, Minnesota is five times as large with 468,000 square yards.

Britain's Metro Centre mall in Newcastle and France's Belle Epine outside Paris both have more floor space than Centro, but the all-in-one combination of shops, offices, hotels, restaurants and sports and concert facilities is new.

In a country like Germany, that cherishes and protects its small merchants, the emergence of such a mega mall has raised fears. Complaining loudest have been neighbouring cities worried about tax revenues being drained away by the new mall and local shopkeepers nervous about losing customers.
"The losses are going to hurt a lot," said Hans-Ulrich Predeick, the city planner in nearby Muelheim. "Centro is going to be a considerable burden for all the neighbouring towns."

Ironically, the trend toward bigger shopping malls in Germany traces its roots to the formerly communist east, where large new centre have risen on the green outskirts of town as retailers fled the high costs of the inner city.
